title: What you are about to see
blurb: This project is building a small language model that thinks in careful steps. This first part shows what it is, how to read the colours and tags, and the words you will need.

scenes.heading: A research project, not a product

caption.text: This is a research project. It is building a language model: a program that reads text and writes an answer.
The aim is a model that learns skills and careful step-by-step thinking from only a few examples.
It is not an app. The project page shows 0 releases, and nothing here is finished.

scenes.heading: The problem, in plain words

caption.text: Most AI models are huge. They keep billions of learned numbers (called parameters) and read mountains of text.
We are testing the opposite: a small, clever design that thinks in rounds, one lap after another.
When it needs exact arithmetic, it asks an ordinary calculator instead of guessing.

scenes.heading: The whole machine in one picture

caption.text: The reader reads the question once and gives each letter a meaning. We borrowed it and cannot change it.
The thinker thinks in rounds. Its settings were set from scratch by our own practice.
The calculator is ordinary code, not AI. It gets a request as text and replies with text.
The stop switch says done. It is built, but was never run.
The talker writes the final answer. Today it is only a small stand-in.

The calculator adds zero learned numbers: it is plain code. This 100M-size model is planned; it has not been trained yet.

scenes.heading: One picture for the whole video

caption.text: One picture runs through the whole video: a student doing a word problem.
A translator reads the question. A team of note-takers thinks it over, round after round.
The team leader writes a request slip. A pocket calculator hands back a slip with the result.
A little bell rings when they are done. One person writes the final answer. Each colour always means the same part.

scenes.heading: Who wrote it? Hand-written or learned

caption.text: Brown means hand-written: a person typed the code. The calculator is like this. Send it sub 12 5 and it sends back 7.
Blue means learned: found by the model's own practice, not typed by a person. The thinker's numbers are like this.
Project rule: everything inside the model is learned. Hand-written code may only run as a tool the model chooses to call.

scenes.heading: Two words: vector and round

caption.text: A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card. The reader turns each letter into one.
A round is one lap: look at the whole question, pass notes, think. The thinker does several laps.

scenes.heading: Two more words: call and reply

caption.text: A call is a request to the calculator, written as text. Here, sub 12 5 means: take 5 away from 12.
The reply is the calculator's answer, also text: 7. Together they read sub 12 5 = 7.
The model writes calls itself. It may also write nothing, when no exact arithmetic is needed.

scenes.heading: Two more words: practice and kept aside

caption.text: Practice: the model tries a question, is told the right answer, and every setting is nudged a tiny bit. One nudge is one update.
Questions kept aside are never used in practice. They are saved for the exam, so the score is fair.

scenes.heading: Score and copy

caption.text: A score is points out of 100: the share of questions answered right. Here, 73.01 points on 6,040 questions kept aside.
A copy is one separate run of the model from its own random start. Six copies are six chances to see the same result.
Careful: 73.01 is one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design.

scenes.heading: The plain model: our yardstick

caption.text: A plain model is an ordinary model of the same size, trained on the same practice. It is the yardstick we compare against.
On the same 6,040 questions kept aside, the plain model scored 67.12 and ours scored 73.01.
Careful: this is one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design. We do not claim it holds at bigger sizes.
